lead: Levelling finds how high one point stands above another, and contouring turns a set of those heights into a picture of the ground's shape. After this unit you can set up and adjust a level, run differential, fly and profile levelling, book and reduce the readings by both standard methods, correct for curvature and refraction, and read a contour map for slope, section and volume.
about: The unit starts with the three words every levelling problem uses: datum, benchmark and reduced level. Chapter 3.1 fixes that reference surface, 3.2 adjusts the instrument that sights along it, 3.3 runs the survey in three field patterns, and 3.4 turns the readings into a checked table of reduced levels. Chapter 3.5, taught by only a few universities, handles the two errors that grow with sight length and the reciprocal method that cancels them. Chapter 3.6 joins points of equal height into contours and reads slope from their spacing, and 3.7, also advanced, turns contour areas into volumes and a reservoir capacity curve.

chapters.idea: A levelling survey is a chain of height differences tied to one fixed surface, and datum, benchmark and reduced level are the words that keep that chain consistent.
chapters.depth: Define level surface, level line, horizontal line, vertical line, mean sea level (MSL), datum, benchmark and reduced level (RL), with the symbol used for each. Types of benchmark: GTS, permanent, temporary and arbitrary. Define height of instrument, backsight (BS), intermediate sight (IS), foresight (FS), change point and station. State the sign convention: RL is height above the datum. Show one step of the chain: RL of a new point = RL of benchmark + BS − FS. Some syllabi call the RL the elevation of the point.

figure.title: One step of the height chain
figure.aria: A downward chain from mean sea level to a benchmark of known reduced level, then to the height of instrument by adding the backsight, and finally to the reduced level of point A by subtracting the foresight.

chapters.example: A benchmark has RL 50.00 m. A level set between the benchmark and a point A reads 2.50 m on the benchmark staff and 1.80 m on the staff at A. Find the height of instrument and the RL of A. Height of instrument = 50.00 + 2.50 = 52.50 m. RL of A = 52.50 − 1.80 = 50.70 m. Check: the ground at A is 2.50 − 1.80 = 0.70 m above the benchmark, and 50.00 + 0.70 = 50.70 m.
chapters.trap: Treating the level line and the horizontal line as the same thing. The level line is curved, the horizontal line is straight and tangent to it, and the instrument sights the horizontal line. Also calling every staff station a benchmark: a benchmark has a known RL fixed by a previous survey, a staff station does not.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, chapter on datums and coordinate systems (MSL, geoid, ellipsoid) and the chapter on maps and scales.
chapters.leave: Trigonometric levelling and height from a vertical angle to Unit 4; GNSS ellipsoidal heights and geoid models to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A level gives a truly horizontal sight only when its geometry is correct, so temporary adjustment makes it correct for the day and permanent adjustment makes it correct for life.
chapters.depth: Name the parts: telescope, eyepiece, objective, diaphragm, plate (tube) bubble, circular bubble, foot screws, levelling head, focusing screw, and the compensator of an automatic level. Temporary adjustment as an ordered routine: setting up, rough levelling with the circular bubble by moving the legs, precise levelling with the plate bubble and three foot screws, focusing the eyepiece, focusing the object, removing parallax, rechecking the bubble. Permanent adjustment: the two-peg test for bubble axis parallel to the line of collimation, the cross-hair verticality check, and the levelling-head check. Some syllabi call this peg adjustment.

figure.title: Temporary adjustment, in order
figure.aria: A six-step downward flowchart of the temporary adjustment of a level, ending with parallax removal, followed by the two-peg test that belongs to permanent adjustment.

chapters.example: Two pegs A and B are 60 m apart. With the level at the midpoint (equal sights, so the error cancels), the readings are 1.500 m on A and 2.100 m on B. True difference = 2.100 − 1.500 = 0.600 m, B below A. The level is moved to 5 m from A: the readings are 1.450 m on A and 2.000 m on B, giving 0.550 m. The far sight is short by 0.600 − 0.550 = 0.050 m, so the correct reading on B is 2.000 + 0.050 = 2.050 m. The cross-hair is raised or lowered until B reads 2.050 m, which makes the bubble axis parallel to the line of collimation.
chapters.trap: Doing permanent adjustment before temporary adjustment. A level that is out of level, or not focused for parallax, gives false two-peg results and you adjust a correct instrument. Also touching the foot screws after focusing, which moves the bubble again.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for backsight, foresight, height of instrument and RL.
chapters.leave: Theodolite temporary and permanent adjustments to Unit 4; the electronics inside a compensator are not needed here.

chapters.idea: The same backsight-minus-foresight arithmetic is repeated in three patterns: one long chain (differential), a quick link (fly) and a line of closely spaced points (profile).
chapters.depth: Differential levelling for distant or high points, with change points and as many setups as needed; simple and compound levelling. Fly levelling as a link between two benchmarks with backsights and foresights only, used for a quick check or to bring a level to the work. Check levelling, returning to the starting benchmark and comparing the closing error with the allowable limit. Profile levelling: longitudinal section at fixed chainage, and cross-sections at right angles for a road or canal. Field rules: keep sights short and balanced, keep the staff vertical, change point staff must not move between foresight and the next backsight. Some syllabi call fly levelling loose levelling or connecting levelling.

figure.title: Which levelling pattern
figure.aria: A flowchart splitting a levelling run into differential, fly and profile levelling, with all three feeding into one booking and reduction step.

chapters.example: Find the RL of point Q from a benchmark of RL 50.00 m, using one change point. Setup 1: BS on benchmark 1.500 m, FS on the change point 2.000 m. Setup 2: BS on the change point 1.200 m, FS on Q 1.700 m. Setup 1 gives HI = 51.500 m and change point RL = 49.500 m. Setup 2 gives HI = 50.700 m and Q RL = 49.000 m. Arithmetic check: ΣBS − ΣFS = (1.500 + 1.200) − (2.000 + 1.700) = 2.700 − 3.700 = −1.000 m, and last RL − first RL = 49.000 − 50.000 = −1.000 m. The run closes in arithmetic, and Q is 1.000 m below the benchmark.
chapters.trap: Calling a fly levelling run a check when it ends on a different benchmark. Only a run that returns to the benchmark it started from, or to a second benchmark of known RL, measures the closing error.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2: RL, height of instrument, and an instrument that is in adjustment.
chapters.leave: Trigonometric levelling by vertical angle to Unit 4; levelling over water for soundings to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A field book must turn staff readings into reduced levels in a fixed layout so the arithmetic can be checked twice before leaving the site.
chapters.depth: Two layouts. Height of collimation (HI) method: HI = RL + BS, RL = HI − IS or FS, a fresh HI at every change point. Rise and fall method: compare consecutive readings, a smaller reading after a larger one is a rise, the reverse is a fall, and RL = previous RL ± rise or fall. Arithmetic checks for both: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL; intermediate sights appear in neither sum. Merits and demerits: HI is quicker to work, rise and fall shows the exact line in which a mistake was made, so it is used for profile and cross-section work. Some syllabi name the HI method the collimation method.

figure.title: One page of a levelling field book
figure.aria: A levelling field book with columns for backsight, intermediate sight, foresight, rise, fall and reduced level, showing a rise of 0.70 to station A and a fall of 0.30 to station B.

chapters.example: Benchmark RL 50.00 m. Readings: 2.50 m on the benchmark (BS), 1.80 m on A (IS), 2.10 m on B (FS). Height of collimation = 50.00 + 2.50 = 52.50 m. RL of A = 52.50 − 1.80 = 50.70 m. RL of B = 52.50 − 2.10 = 50.40 m. By rise and fall: 2.50 to 1.80 is a rise of 0.70 m, 1.80 to 2.10 is a fall of 0.30 m. Checks: ΣBS − ΣFS = 2.50 − 2.10 = 0.40 m; ΣRise − ΣFall = 0.70 − 0.30 = 0.40 m; last RL − first RL = 50.40 − 50.00 = 0.40 m.
chapters.trap: Writing a rise where the next reading is larger and a fall belongs. The reading tells you the height of the line of sight above the ground; a bigger reading means lower ground. Also putting intermediate sights into the ΣBS − ΣFS check, which then fails on a correct book.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 to 3.3: the terms, the instrument and the field patterns that produce the readings.
chapters.leave: Total station and digital data logging to Unit 5; least-squares adjustment of a whole levelling network to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Over long sights the curved earth drops the staff and the atmosphere bends the line of sight, so the two corrections are combined, and reciprocal levelling cancels whatever error is left.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Curvature correction Cc = 0.0785 d² metres, refraction Cr = 0.0112 d² metres, combined correction = 0.0673 d² metres, with d in kilometres and R taken as 6370 km; the combined correction is subtracted from the staff reading. Sketch the geometry for d²/2R. Reciprocal levelling across a river: with the instrument near A read the near staff (rA) and the far staff (rB), repeat with the instrument near B (r′A, r′B), and take h = ½[(rB − rA) + (r′B − r′A)]. The remaining half-difference is the error in one far sight.

figure.aria: Two rising curves against sight length: the curvature correction reaching 0.314 metres at 2 kilometres and the combined curvature plus refraction correction reaching 0.269 metres at the same distance.

chapters.example: A river is about 1.2 km wide and levels are taken across it by reciprocal levelling. Level near A: reading on A 1.500 m, reading on B 2.900 m. Level near B: reading on B 2.800 m, reading on A 1.600 m. First apparent difference = 2.900 − 1.500 = 1.400 m, second = 2.800 − 1.600 = 1.200 m. True difference h = ½(1.400 + 1.200) = 1.300 m, with A higher than B. The far sight carries an error of ½(1.400 − 1.200) = 0.100 m; for 1.2 km the formula gives 0.0673 × 1.2² = 0.097 m, and the small remainder is a collimation error.
chapters.trap: Putting d in metres into 0.0785 d². The constant is built for kilometres; a 200 m sight is d = 0.2 km and gives 0.003 m, not 3140 m. Also adding the correction to the staff reading when it must be subtracted.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.3 and 3.4: differential levelling with change points, and the booking of backsights and foresights.
chapters.leave: Trigonometric and tacheometric heighting to Unit 4; the physics of atmospheric refraction to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A contour is a line of constant reduced level, so a contoured map is the shape of the ground flattened onto paper and its spacing reads directly as slope.
chapters.depth: Definitions: contour, contour interval (some syllabi call it the vertical interval), horizontal equivalent, and the factors that fix the interval — purpose, scale, ground slope and time. Characteristics: contours of different levels never meet except at a cliff or an overhang; they form closed loops or run off the sheet; close spacing is steep ground, wide spacing is flat ground; evenly spaced contours are a uniform slope; a contour crossing a valley bends upstream, one crossing a ridge bends downstream; contours never cross a building or a vertical cut. Methods: direct, and indirect by cross-sections, grid squares, tacheometry or radial lines, with interpolation between spot levels. Uses: site selection, road and canal alignment, drainage, reservoir siting, cut and fill, and sections from a map.

figure.title: Ways to contour a site
figure.aria: A flowchart of contouring methods: direct contouring on the left, and indirect contouring on the right, which splits into cross-sections, grid squares and tacheometric methods.

chapters.example: Two grid points are 30 m apart. Their reduced levels are 102.6 m and 105.1 m, and the contour interval is 2 m, so the contours to be drawn are 104 m and (if it falls inside) 106 m. The 104 m contour lies at a distance x from the first point, found by proportion: x = (104 − 102.6)/(105.1 − 102.6) × 30 = 1.4/2.5 × 30 = 16.8 m from the point of RL 102.6 m.
chapters.trap: Saying the V of a contour in a valley points downstream. Water flows down the valley and the contour bends upstream, so the V points towards higher ground. Also quoting one contour interval for all maps: a 1:1000 site plan takes 0.25 to 0.5 m, a 1:50 000 topographic sheet takes 10 or 20 m.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for reduced level, and Unit 1 for map scale and topographic sheets.
chapters.leave: Contour generation from a DEM and raster surfaces to Unit 7; contouring with a total station or GNSS to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Each contour encloses an area at a known level, so measuring those areas gives volumes by the trapezoidal or prismoidal rule and a reservoir capacity curve.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Area enclosed by a contour from a planimeter or from coordinates of the traced contour. Volume from successive contour areas with interval h: trapezoidal V = h(A₁ + A₂)/2 for one slice, prismoidal V = h(A₁ + 4Am + A₂)/6 when a mid-area is known. Capacity of a reservoir from contour areas at successive elevations, summed from the lowest contour upward, giving the capacity–elevation curve and the dead storage below the lowest draw-off. Conclude with the capacity at full supply level and the volume between two levels, which is the storage between them.

figure.aria: A capacity against elevation curve rising from 16 thousand cubic metres at 102 metres to 98 thousand cubic metres at 106 metres.

chapters.example: A reservoir site is contoured at a 2 m interval. Areas enclosed: 0.4 ha at 100 m, 1.2 ha at 102 m, 2.0 ha at 104 m and 3.0 ha at 106 m. Slice 100 to 102 m: V = 2 × (0.4 + 1.2)/2 = 1.6 ha·m = 16 000 m³. Slice 102 to 104 m: V = 2 × (1.2 + 2.0)/2 = 3.2 ha·m, cumulative 4.8 ha·m = 48 000 m³. Slice 104 to 106 m: V = 2 × (2.0 + 3.0)/2 = 5.0 ha·m, cumulative 9.8 ha·m = 98 000 m³. The capacity at 106 m is 98 000 m³.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that 1 hectare = 10 000 m², so an answer in ha·m is 10 000 times the volume in m³. Also using the prismoidal formula with an area that was never measured at the middle level.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.6 for contours and their spacing, and Unit 2 for area computation by coordinates.
chapters.leave: Earthwork for roads, mass haul diagrams and cut-and-fill balancing go beyond this unit; DEM-based volume in GIS to Unit 7.
